BUS.G12.T2.SECTORENV.A1.title: Business sector and its environment
BUS.G12.T2.SECTORENV.A1.description: Selecting a business from each economic sector and describing the three business environments related to those sectors and the extent to which a business can control each environment.
BUS.G12.T2.SECTORENV.A1.strand: T2 — CSR, human rights, teams, sector & environment, leadership & quality
BUS.G12.T2.SECTORENV.A1.recovery_strategy: Whatever the sector (primary, secondary, tertiary), the rule holds: full control of the micro environment, influence over the market, no control over the macro environment.

questions.question: A gold mine belongs to which sector?
questions.memo: A mine extracts raw materials, so it is a primary-sector business.

questions.question: How much control does a business have over its micro environment?
questions.memo: The micro environment is inside the business — its mission, structure, resources and culture — so the business controls it fully, in any sector.

questions.question: True or false: A business has no control over its macro environment, whatever its sector.
questions.memo: The macro environment is beyond any business's control, regardless of whether it is primary, secondary or tertiary.

questions.question: A bank belongs to the _________ sector.
questions.memo: A bank provides a service, so it is a tertiary-sector business.

questions.question: A car-assembly factory belongs to the _________ sector.
questions.memo: A factory processes materials into products, making it a secondary-sector business.

questions.question: True or false: In every sector, a business can influence but not control its market environment.
questions.memo: Across all sectors, the market environment can only be influenced (e.g. by advertising or negotiating), not controlled.

questions.question: Sort each business into the correct sector.
questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Farms and fishing extract (primary); factories and mills process (secondary); travel agencies and brokers serve (tertiary).

questions.question: Which statement correctly describes a business's control across the three environments?
options: Full control of the micro, influence over the market, no control of the macro
Full control of all three environments
Control of the macro but not the micro
questions.expected: Full control of the micro, influence over the market, no control of the macro
questions.memo: Control decreases outward: full (micro), influence (market), none (macro) — the same in every sector.

questions.question: Read both businesses, then decide which each statement matches.

source_a.text: We are a wheat farm in the primary sector. We control how we run the farm, but we cannot control rainfall or world grain prices.

source_b.text: We are a logistics company in the tertiary sector. We control our own operations, but we cannot control the fuel price or new transport laws.

questions.memo: The farm is primary, the logistics firm tertiary; both control their micro environment but not the macro, and neither controls the economy.

questions.question: A business can _________ its market environment but not control it.
questions.memo: The market environment can be influenced through actions like advertising and negotiation, but not controlled.

questions.question: Why does the same control rule apply to businesses in all three sectors?
options: The three environments work the same way no matter what a business produces or sells
Sectors change the laws of the macro environment
questions.expected: The three environments work the same way no matter what a business produces or sells
questions.memo: Whatever a business makes or sells, its micro is controllable, its market influenceable and its macro uncontrollable.

questions.question: True or false: A primary-sector mine can control global commodity prices.
questions.memo: Global commodity prices are a macro force; even a large mine cannot control them — it can only adapt.

questions.question: Sort each factor by how much control a tertiary retailer has over it.

items.text: Its own store layout and staff

questions.expected: All six items in correct buckets (or ≥75%)
questions.memo: Store layout and pricing are micro; suppliers and competitors are market; interest rates and laws are macro.

questions.question: Which is a macro-environment factor that could affect a tertiary tourism business?
options: A change in the exchange rate affecting foreign visitors
Its own choice of staff uniforms
The layout of its reception desk
questions.expected: A change in the exchange rate affecting foreign visitors
questions.memo: The exchange rate is a macro force the tourism business cannot control but must adapt to; the others are internal (micro).

questions.question: How does a business in any sector respond to its macro environment?
options: By adapting, since it cannot control macro forces
By controlling the macro forces directly
By passing laws to change them
questions.expected: By adapting, since it cannot control macro forces
questions.memo: Because macro forces are beyond control, a business in any sector responds by adapting its own plans.

questions.question: The _________ environment is the one inside the business that it controls fully.
questions.memo: The micro environment — vision, structure, resources, culture — is internal and fully controlled by the business.

questions.question: Read both businesses, then decide which each statement matches.

source_a.text: Our steel mill (secondary sector) can decide how we run our plant, and we negotiate hard with suppliers, but new import tariffs are out of our hands.

source_b.text: Our accounting firm (tertiary sector) controls how we serve clients and which software we use, but we cannot control new tax legislation.

statements.text: Provides a professional service to clients

questions.memo: The mill influences suppliers (market); the firm serves clients; both control their micro operations; neither controls legislation (macro).

questions.question: A learner claims, 'A big enough company in any sector can eventually control its macro environment.' How is this best evaluated?
options: Incorrect — no business, however large, controls the macro environment; it can only influence and adapt
Correct — size grants full macro control
Correct, but only in the primary sector
questions.expected: Incorrect — no business, however large, controls the macro environment; it can only influence and adapt
questions.memo: Size may give influence (e.g. lobbying), but the macro environment remains beyond control for every business and sector.

questions.question: Why is it useful to compare a primary, a secondary and a tertiary business when studying the environments?
options: It shows the control rule holds across sectors, even though the specific factors differ
It proves each sector controls a different environment fully
It shows only one sector has a macro environment
It removes the need to study the environments
questions.expected: It shows the control rule holds across sectors, even though the specific factors differ
questions.memo: Comparing sectors demonstrates that the micro/market/macro control pattern is universal, while the particular factors vary by business.

questions.question: A tertiary delivery firm faces rising fuel prices, tough competitors and outdated vehicles. How should it map these to the environments?
options: Fuel prices = macro (adapt), competitors = market (influence), vehicles = micro (control)
All three are macro and uncontrollable
All three are micro and fully controlled
questions.expected: Fuel prices = macro (adapt), competitors = market (influence), vehicles = micro (control)
questions.memo: Fuel prices are macro (adapt), competitors are market (influence), and its own vehicles are micro (control) — the standard pattern.
